title: European leaders warn Russia's war on Ukraine spilling over their borders
transcript:
Speaker 1: Nine EU member states will meet in Brussels today as European leaders warn Russia's war on Ukraine is spilling over their borders.
Speaker 1: Over the weekend, a Russian cargo ship was hit by drones in the Gulf of Finland with the Finnish Defense Forces blaming Ukraine for the attack.
Speaker 1: And Poland has accused Russia of violating its airspace during an attack on Ukraine, saying it coincided with European military drills in the country.
Speaker 1: It comes amid an escalation in fighting between Russia and Ukraine and as the United States reportedly pushes for the warring parties to reach a peace deal before January.
Speaker 1: Scott Lucas is professor of International Politics at University College, Dublin.
Speaker 1: Why is this meeting being called?
Speaker 1: What's it expected to achieve?
Scott Lucas: Well, I mean the catalyst for this meeting is what you just mentioned, which is these two Russian missiles and a drone, which landed in Poland, which is a NATO member over the weekend.
Scott Lucas: Although the Russians have previously had munitions, which have landed in Poland.
Scott Lucas: It's been assessed that in those cases it was simply those that have sort of strayed and gone beyond the Russian targets inside Ukraine.
Scott Lucas: In this case, the Polish authorities believe that the Russian attack was intentional.
Scott Lucas: Sort of a demonstration attack because there was an 11-country military exercise being hosted by Poland.
Scott Lucas: Indeed, it was only about 60 to 70 kilometers away from where the munitions landed.
Scott Lucas: Well, under NATO's charter, you know, if you have an attack on one member, the others are obligated to come to its defense under Article 5.
Scott Lucas: I don't think this meeting of the North Atlantic Council will go as far on Monday as to declare that we are at a position where there has effectively been an expansion of Russia's war on Ukraine to a NATO member.
Scott Lucas: But I think NATO is having to make preparations not only for drones and missiles, but for what we might call hybrid warfare.
Scott Lucas: Because for months, and indeed for years, the Russians have been carrying out cyber warfare, they've been carrying out wartime, sorry, operations at sea with their shadow fleet at times threatening vital undersea cables.
Scott Lucas: And they have been carrying out sabotage operations, including an attack in August in which a drone nearly detonated beside a Ukraine cargo plane in Leipzig Airport.
Speaker 1: The Finnish Prime Minister calls Ukraine's drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in its waters as an escalation.
Speaker 1: Is it?
Scott Lucas: Yeah, I think you, you know, we need to look at this from all sides and that is that Finnish authorities believe that the attack on this Russian ship, effectively a, you know, an auxiliary ship of the Russian military, and has badly damaged it.
Scott Lucas: That raises questions of even as you're defending Ukraine, even as you're defending um, them against a Russian invasion, which may be taking its last best shot this winter to try to force Kiev's surrender.
Scott Lucas: How far can Ukraine go in its counter attacks against Russian industries?
Speaker 1: There's been a concerted effort in recent months and weeks by the US and others to progress peace talks and bring an end to the almost five-year conflict.
Speaker 1: Could these latest developments threaten progress towards a peace deal?
Scott Lucas: No, because that peace deal wasn't going to be achieved.
Scott Lucas: I mean, I need to be very honest with you here, which is you've got three actors here.
Scott Lucas: You've got the Russians who are refusing to discuss a ceasefire on the current front lines in Ukraine.
Scott Lucas: They are refusing to discuss a territorial settlement in which they may not be able to grab, seize more Ukrainian territory, and they're refusing to discuss security guarantees for Kiev.
Scott Lucas: Instead, they are saying, well, have a European wide, European wide security architecture, which will be agreed between them and NATO, but which will prohibit, ban NATO from being able to defend Ukraine.
Scott Lucas: You have Ukraine on the other hand, backed by the European partners, and indeed to an extent by other countries such as Australia, who is saying, look, we we have to have a ceasefire.
Scott Lucas: You have to have a ceasefire.
Scott Lucas: That's the first priority.
Scott Lucas: You cannot surrender more territory to Russia just because they demand it.
Scott Lucas: And our security is paramount.
Scott Lucas: The problem with the Americans is is that they're not any even hand broker between the two sides.
Scott Lucas: And that is because the Kremlin has offered, uh, Donald Trump's envoys, the real estate developer Steve Witkoff, his son-in-law Jared Kushner, tens of billions of dollars in deals.
Scott Lucas: Indeed, Vladimir Putin's financial fixer, Kirill Dmitriev, is speaking of trillions of dollars of deals.
Scott Lucas: And those deals, which were put to Kushner and Witkoff, uh, at the start of September, actually benefit friends and associates and family of Donald Trump, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Scott Lucas: In other words, these folks want a ceasefire.
Scott Lucas: This Trump camp wants a ceasefire to a large part because they want economic projects with the Russians.
Scott Lucas: And that means that to a large extent, they're promoting the Kremlin's agenda rather than one in which Ukraine would achieve the ceasefire that it wants.
